data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The 'shown-to-fail-first' installation is not a neutral ritual but a bias: it makes the registry count the first failure it sees, so the test constrains its subject exactly when the subject's guard is slow relative to the test, and describes it when the guard is fast; the 3-of-26 result is a latency race, not a coverage measure.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If guard and test latencies were equalised and the 3-of-26 result persisted, the race explanation would be refuted.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a surviving mutation's guard could be shown to have completed before the test's failure signal, the race claim would fail for that case.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the registry recorded both the guard verdict and the test failure with timestamps, the race would become directly testable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Under fail-first installation, the winner of the race between the guard's evaluation and the test's failure writes the registry entry. The 3 survivors are the cases where the guard would have fired but the test's failure channel was faster, so the registry records the test's description. The compile.py 1/9 and the 4/4 to 6/7 banding are the race outcomes across modules with different guard latencies.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
